topic: Performance metrics: execution time, clock rate and CPI
title: Measure cycles and CPI, then make the loop faster
instructions:
## Execution time = instructions × CPI × clock period

The starter program computes **total = 8 × (sum of nums)**. It works, but it is slow: it multiplies inside the loop and adds to memory on every pass.

The bench charges cycles per instruction (open "Instruction set and cycle costs"): 1 for MOV, ALU and shift instructions, 10 for MUL, 2 for a taken jump or LOOP and 1 for one that falls through, plus 2 for any operand in memory.

## Do this

1. **Run to HLT** on the starter, before changing anything. Read the instruction and cycle counts and answer the four questions. Assume a 4 MHz clock.
2. Rewrite the program so it still stores the right **total** for any eight values, in **at most 70 cycles**. Keep the running sum in a register, and remember that multiplying by 8 is a shift left by 3.

config.starter:
; total = 8 x (sum of nums), the slow way.
nums:  DW 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6
total: DW 0

        MOV SI, 0
        MOV CX, 8
next:   MOV AX, [nums+SI]   ; load a value
        MOV BX, 8
        MUL BX              ; multiply it by 8
        ADD [total], AX     ; add it to total in memory
        INC SI
        LOOP next
        HLT

hints: CPI is cycles ÷ instructions. Time is cycles ÷ clock rate: 162 cycles at 4 MHz is 162 × 0.25 µs.
Add every value into AX inside the loop, and multiply once after the loop.
SHL AX, 3 costs 1 cycle; MUL costs 10. Store into [total] once, after the loop.

realityNote: Compilers make the same moves: strength reduction turns multiplication by a power of two into a shift, and register allocation keeps a running sum out of memory. Real CPUs hide some costs with pipelining and caches, but the instruction count × CPI × clock period equation still governs.
